Painted in 1926 by Kshitindranath Majumdar, 'Rasa-Lila' is one of the most spiritually radiant and lyrical achievements of the Bengal School wash tradition. Majumdar, who was revered as a 'Bhakta-Shilpi' (Saint-Artist) for his lifelong devotional immersion in the Chaitanya Mahaprabhu Vaishnava faith, translates the mystical Maha-Rasa of Vrindavana into a celestial visual reverie. Majumdar's figures are distinguished by their extraordinary elongated grace, slender willow-like waists, and sinuous undulating lines that sway with musical cadence. The flowering branches of Kadamba trees drape over the dancers, framing the ecstatic circular dance against translucent, pastel washes of pale mauve, soft saffron, and dusky blue, conserved in the National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi.

The Bengal School of Painting emerged in the first decade of the 20th century as the powerful visual wing of the anti-partition Swadeshi movement. Led by Ernest Binfield (E.B.) Havell, the visionary Principal of the Government School of Art, Calcutta, and Abanindranath Tagore, who became Vice-Principal in 1905, the movement launched a radical aesthetic rebellion against Western academic realism. Havell took the controversial step of removing European plaster casts from the school and exhibiting Mughal, Rajput, and Ajanta masterpieces, urging Indian students to draw spiritual inspiration from their own civilizational heritage. Supported by Sister Nivedita, Ananda K. Painted in 1940 by Ramgopal Vijaivargiya using watercolor on paper, 'Meghdoot' is a celebrated masterpiece inspired by the immortal Sanskrit lyric poem Meghadutam (The Cloud Messenger) composed by classical poet Kalidasa. A student of Shailendranath Dey at the Jaipur Art School, Vijaivargiya transplanted the lyrical Bengal wash style into Rajasthan, fusing it with classical Sanskrit literature. The painting portrays the exiled Yaksha, banished by Lord Kubera to Mount Ramgiri for neglecting his duties. Seated on a high rocky crag, the Yaksha is depicted pleading with a billowing, dark monsoon cloud to carry his message of eternal love and fidelity across the plains of India to his pining wife in the distant Himalayan city of Alakapuri. In his hands, the Yaksha reverently holds fresh wild Kutaja blossoms as an offering to the cloud, while a flock of white cranes (balaka) soars gracefully against the slate-blue rain clouds, heralding the joyous onset of the monsoon, conserved in the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), New Delhi.
